title: In which scenarios would you specifically need `StringBuffer` over `StringBuilder`?
shortTitle: When would you specifically need StringBuffer over StringBuilder?

s1_definition.profdef: You need `StringBuffer` instead of `StringBuilder` only in the specific scenario where a single mutable character buffer instance is shared and mutated by more than one thread at the same time, and you want the individual append, insert, and delete operations to be internally synchronized so the buffer is not corrupted. `StringBuffer` marks every mutating method as synchronized, so concurrent calls are serialized on the buffer's intrinsic lock. `StringBuilder` is the same API without that locking, so it is faster but unsafe under concurrent mutation. In every single-threaded situation, or when each thread owns its own buffer, `StringBuilder` is the correct default, and `StringBuffer` is reserved for the genuinely shared-mutable-across-threads case.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a single shared logbook sitting on a counter where several clerks must write entries. If many clerks write at once with no rule, the page turns into a scribbled mess with overlapping ink. A StringBuffer is that same logbook but with a single pen chained to it and a rule that only one clerk may hold the pen at a time, so entries never collide. A StringBuilder is the same logbook with no pen rule, which is perfectly fast and fine when only one clerk uses it, but dangerous if several clerks share it. Rajesh and Priya's audit trail is written by many background worker threads into one shared record, and that is exactly the rare place where the bank must chain the pen, meaning use a StringBuffer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reach for StringBuffer only when one mutable buffer instance is appended to by multiple threads concurrently; otherwise always use StringBuilder.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You need `StringBuffer` instead of `StringBuilder` only in the specific scenario where a single mutable character buffer instance is shared and mutated by more than one thread at the same time, and you want the individual append, insert, and delete operations to be internally synchronized so the buffer is not corrupted. `StringBuffer` marks every mutating method as synchronized, so concurrent calls are serialized on the buffer's intrinsic lock. `StringBuilder` is the same API without that locking, so it is faster but unsafe under concurrent mutation. In every single-threaded situation, or when each thread owns its own buffer, `StringBuilder` is the correct default, and `StringBuffer` is reserved for the genuinely shared-mutable-across-threads case.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a single shared logbook sitting on a counter where several clerks must write entries. If many clerks write at once with no rule, the page turns into a scribbled mess with overlapping ink. A StringBuffer is that same logbook but with a single pen chained to it and a rule that only one clerk may hold the pen at a time, so entries never collide. A StringBuilder is the same logbook with no pen rule, which is perfectly fast and fine when only one clerk uses it, but dangerous if several clerks share it. Rajesh and Priya's audit trail is written by many background worker threads into one shared record, and that is exactly the rare place where the bank must chain the pen, meaning use a StringBuffer.

**One line to remember:** Reach for StringBuffer only when one mutable buffer instance is appended to by multiple threads concurrently; otherwise always use StringBuilder.

sections.s2_technical:
The whole decision rests on one question: is a single mutable buffer object mutated by more than one thread at the same time? If the answer is no, which is the overwhelmingly common case, `StringBuilder` is correct because it avoids all locking overhead. If the answer is yes, and you cannot redesign to give each thread its own buffer, then `StringBuffer` is the tool because its synchronized methods make each append atomic and provide memory visibility between threads.

The reason `StringBuffer` is safe is that each public method, for example `append`, acquires the buffer's monitor before touching the internal array and the count field. For instance `sharedBuffer.append(entry)` enters a synchronized block on the StringBuffer instance, so a second thread calling `sharedBuffer.append(other)` must wait, which prevents the two read-modify-write sequences on the count from interleaving and corrupting the array.

A critical senior nuance is that this synchronization only makes each single call atomic, not a sequence of calls. If a thread does `if (buf.length() < limit) buf.append(x);`, another thread can slip in between the `length` check and the `append`, so compound logic still needs external synchronization even with StringBuffer. StringBuffer protects the buffer's internal integrity, not your multi-step business invariants.

The genuinely valid scenarios are narrow. One is a legacy or shared component where one StringBuffer field is deliberately exposed and appended to by multiple threads, such as an older audit accumulator. Another is when an API you must implement hands you a single buffer that concurrent callbacks append to. A third is simply maintaining old code that already uses StringBuffer correctly, where switching brings no benefit. Outside these, the modern and faster pattern is thread-confined StringBuilders, often one per thread via ThreadLocal, whose results are merged at the end, which removes lock contention entirely and outperforms a single shared StringBuffer. So the honest senior answer is that StringBuffer is rarely needed, and its one real justification is a shared mutable buffer across threads.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank runs several background worker threads that all append transaction lines into one shared audit buffer that lives for the duration of a batch run. Because the same buffer object is touched by many threads, the appends must not corrupt each other. This is exactly where StringBuffer's synchronized append gives per-call safety.

Problem 2 — A developer first tried the same shared-single-buffer design using a StringBuilder, and under six concurrent threads the final audit came out with fewer lines than expected because the unsynchronized count field got overwritten during interleaving. This is exactly StringBuilder's lack of thread-safety showing why the shared case needs StringBuffer.

Problem 3 — The better design the senior recommends is giving each worker its own StringBuilder and merging at the end, which is faster and avoids locks. This shows that StringBuffer is the fallback only when a single shared buffer truly cannot be avoided.

The code runs many threads against one shared StringBuffer and one shared StringBuilder, and a `BufferChoiceDemo` main class prints the resulting line counts so the corruption of the unsynchronized shared builder is visible, while also showing the thread-local alternative.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/audit/BufferChoiceDemo.java

# Run (StringBuffer count is exact; shared StringBuilder count is usually short)
java -cp out com.bank.audit.BufferChoiceDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: six worker threads, each appending five hundred audit entries, for an expected total of three thousand lines, into one shared StringBuffer and one shared StringBuilder.

Step 1 — The main thread creates the shared StringBuffer and shared StringBuilder, both empty, and starts six threads. The account id "SAV2001" is a String and is only read, never changed, so it needs no protection.

Step 2 — Each thread builds an entry string like "SAV2001-w3-250" and calls record on both accumulators. For the StringBuffer, the append call grabs the buffer's lock, so even if all six threads call at the same moment, they line up and each append completes fully before the next begins. The count field and backing array stay consistent.

Step 3 — For the StringBuilder, the append call grabs no lock. Two threads can both read the same count value, both write their characters into overlapping positions, and both store a count that ignores the other's write. The result is lost characters and a count smaller than reality.

Step 4 — After the latch reaches zero, the main thread converts each accumulator to a String and counts the lines. The StringBuffer reports exactly three thousand lines. The StringBuilder reports fewer, demonstrating corruption.

Step 5 — The final output shows the exact count for the synchronized buffer and a wrong count for the unsynchronized one, proving that the shared-mutable-across-threads scenario is precisely where StringBuffer earns its place.

```
Oct 30, 2026 3:45:10 PM com.bank.audit.BufferChoiceDemo main
INFO: Expected lines = 3000
Oct 30, 2026 3:45:10 PM com.bank.audit.BufferChoiceDemo main
INFO: Shared StringBuffer lines  = 3000 (CORRECT)
Oct 30, 2026 3:45:10 PM com.bank.audit.BufferChoiceDemo main
WARNING: Shared StringBuilder lines = 2714 (CORRUPTED under concurrency)
Oct 30, 2026 3:45:10 PM com.bank.audit.BufferChoiceDemo main
INFO: Senior recommendation: prefer per-thread StringBuilder merged at end.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The honest answer is that in modern Java you very rarely need StringBuffer, and the one scenario that genuinely requires it is when a single mutable character buffer instance is shared and appended to by more than one thread at the same time, and you want each individual append or insert to be internally safe. StringBuffer achieves that because every mutating method is synchronized on the buffer object, so concurrent calls line up one after another and the internal array and length counter never get corrupted. StringBuilder has exactly the same API but without that synchronization, which makes it faster but unsafe the moment two threads mutate the same instance.

So my decision rule is simple. If the buffer is used by a single thread, which is almost always the case, I use StringBuilder because it avoids locking overhead and is the correct default. If multiple threads mutate one shared buffer and I cannot redesign that away, I use StringBuffer. In our banking system this came up in a batch audit assembler where several worker threads appended transaction lines into one shared buffer. With a shared StringBuilder the final audit lost lines because the unsynchronized length counter got overwritten during interleaving, and switching that shared instance to a StringBuffer fixed the corruption immediately.

The nuance I always add is that StringBuffer only makes each single call atomic, not a sequence of calls, so if my logic checks the length and then appends, another thread can still slip in between, and I would need my own synchronization for that compound step. StringBuffer guards the buffer's internal integrity, not my multi-step business invariants.

The senior point I close with is that even in the multi-threaded case there is usually a better design than a shared StringBuffer. I prefer giving each thread its own StringBuilder, often through a ThreadLocal, and merging the results at the end. That removes lock contention completely and is both correct and faster than everyone fighting over one synchronized buffer. So I treat StringBuffer as a legitimate but narrow tool for a genuinely shared mutable buffer, while my default stays StringBuilder for single-threaded building and thread-confined builders for concurrency.

---

keyPoints: Only when multiple threads append to the same buffer concurrently
Example: shared log buffer written by multiple threads
In practice, extremely rare — most string building is single-threaded
Prefer StringBuilder + external synchronization for clarity
